The Higher Boranes:
Families, Shapes
and Synthesis

From Stock's two homologous series to closo, nido and arachno cages, and how chemists build them.

P. A. Mohammed Ziyad · Department of Chemistry, Farook College (Autonomous), Kozhikode

nido-B10H14 (idealised)
drag to rotate
M. F. Hawthorne, "Boron Hydrides", in The Chemistry of Boron and its Compounds, ed. E. L. Muetterties, Wiley, 1967, ch. 5; A. K. Das, Fundamental Concepts of Inorganic Chemistry, Vol. 5, 2nd edn, §10.12.
Deck 3 moves from diborane to the larger boranes: how they are classified, what shapes they adopt, and how they are made. The 3D models in this deck are idealised: they are built from regular deltahedra with standard bond lengths, so they show topology, not exact crystal geometry.

Orientation slide.
Learning outcomes

By the end of this deck you should be able to

  • Classify a borane as closo, nido, arachno, hypho or conjuncto from its formula, and name it systematically.
  • Name the deltahedra from n = 4 to 12, and derive nido and arachno shapes by removing vertices.
  • Describe the structures of B4H10, B5H9, B5H11, B6H10 and B10H14, with key distances and NMR features.
  • Outline the main synthetic routes: diborane pyrolysis, deprotonation–insertion, discharge methods, and the closo anions.
  • Explain how the (BH)n(BH3)x view accounts for interconversion of boranes.
Das, Vol. 5, §10.12; Hawthorne (1967), §§5.2–5.5.
Read the outcomes.
Part A

Families and names

From Stock's BnHn+4 and BnHn+6 to a classification by cage shape.

A
Part A introduces the classification and nomenclature.
Families and names

Five families, defined by formula

ClassFormulaName meansCageExamples
closoBnHn²⁻ (≡ BnHn+2)cage (Greek)complete deltahedronB6H6²⁻ … B12H12²⁻
nidoBnHn+4nest (Latin nidus)one vertex missingB2H6, B5H9, B6H10, B8H12, B10H14
arachnoBnHn+6spider's web (Greek)two vertices missingB4H10, B5H11, B6H12, B9H15
hyphoBnHn+8net (Greek)three vertices missingB5H12⁻; no neutral example
conjunctofused cagesjoined (Latin)two or more units linkedB10H16, B18H22, B20H16

Stability

Thermal stability generally falls in the order closo > nido > arachno > hypho, and within a series larger members tend to be less stable. A sixth, klado (BnHn+10, "branch"), completes the formal sequence.

Das, Vol. 5, §10.12.1–10.12.3; name origins: Mingos, Struct. Bond. 2021, 187, p. 26; R. E. Williams, Inorg. Chem. 1971, 10, 210.
The formula alone tells you the class. Count H beyond n: +2 (as the dianion) is closo, +4 nido, +6 arachno, +8 hypho. Students should practise with B6H10 (nido) and B9H15 (arachno).
Families and names

A bookkeeping view: (BH)n(BH3)x

  • Any borane BpHp+q can be written as BH units plus BH3 units.
  • nido boranes contain x = 2 (q = 4). arachno boranes contain x = 3 (q = 6).
  • Interconversions then become simple arithmetic: gain or loss of BH3, and loss of H2 (BH3 → BH + H2).
Borane(BH)n(BH3)xclass
B2H6(BH3)2nido
B3H7(BH)(BH3)2nido (unstable)
B5H9(BH)3(BH3)2nido
B10H14(BH)8(BH3)2nido
B4H10(BH)(BH3)3arachno
B6H12(BH)3(BH3)3arachno
Das, Vol. 5, §10.12.1 (note) and §10.12.8(c).
This is a formal decomposition, not a structure. It is useful in Part D to rationalise pyrolysis: for example, B2H6 + BH3 → B3H9 → B3H7 + H2.
Families and names

Naming boranes and borane anions

Neutral boranes

  • Greek prefix for the number of B: di, tri, tetra, penta, hexa, hepta, octa, ennea (9), deca …
  • Arabic number in brackets for the number of H.
  • B5H9: pentaborane(9); B5H11: pentaborane(11); B9H15: enneaborane(15); B14H20: tetradecaborane(20).
  • Diborane(6) is usually just "diborane".

Anions (hydroborates)

  • Count H and B separately, with the charge in brackets.
  • B5H8⁻: octahydropentaborate(1−)
  • B10H10²⁻: decahydrodecaborate(2−)
  • B12H12²⁻: dodecahydrododecaborate(2−)

Adding the structural prefix

octahydro-nido-pentaborate(1−) · dodecahydro-closo-dodecaborate(2−) · nido-decaborane(14). Atoms are numbered from the apex down, ring by ring.

Das, Vol. 5, §10.12.2; IUPAC, Nomenclature of Inorganic Chemistry (Red Book), 2005, IR-6.
Point out "ennea" for nine, which students often get wrong (not "nona" in older literature). The bracketed number distinguishes the two pentaboranes.
Part B

Building with deltahedra

Every closo borane is a triangulated polyhedron. Nido and arachno shapes are the same polyhedra with corners removed.

B
Part B: geometry. The deltahedra, and the vertex-removal idea of Williams (1971).
Building with deltahedra · history

Icosahedral fragments (1950s) or deltahedral families (1971)?

Lipscomb's view (1950s–60s)

  • Most boranes look like fragments of an icosahedron: B10H14, B6H10, B9H15 …
  • B5H9 and B4H10 fit an octahedron better.
  • This works, but does not say which fragment a given formula will adopt.

Williams' view (1971)

  • Start from the complete deltahedron of the closo anion BnHn²⁻.
  • Remove the most highly connected vertex to get the nido shape, then an adjacent one to get arachno.
  • One rule now links formula to shape. Wade (1971) added the electron count (Deck 6).
"…it should at least serve as a convenient memory aid in the teaching of the subject."R. E. Williams, Inorg. Chem. 1971, on his own proposal (quoted by Mingos 2021)
R. E. Williams, Inorg. Chem. 1971, 10, 210; Hawthorne (1967), §5.2, p. 231; Mingos (2021), §7, pp. 25–26, Fig. 16.
Williams' proposal is the structural half of the modern picture; Wade supplied the electronic half in the same year. Note the honest closing line of Williams' paper. One known exception: B8H12 is closer to arachno-B9H15 than to a nido-B9 shape.
Building with deltahedra

The closo deltahedra, n = 4 to 12

n = 12 · icosahedron · Ih
drag to rotate
ndeltahedronfacesedgescloso anion
5trigonal bipyramid69B5H5²⁻ (C2B3H5)
6octahedron812B6H6²⁻

12icosahedron2030B12H12²⁻

Euler: V − E + F = 2. For any deltahedron F = 2V − 4 and E = 3V − 6. Edges are geometric, not 2c–2e bonds.

Das, Vol. 5, §10.12.3, Fig. 10.12.3.1; Williams (1971); models: idealised equilateral-edge deltahedra (n = 11 has unequal edges in reality).
Click through n = 4 to 12. Point out the vertex connectivities: 4 and 5 for most, with a unique 6-connected vertex at n = 11. The lines are edges of the polyhedron, not localised bonds; bonding is delocalised (Deck 6).
Building with deltahedra

Remove a vertex: closo → nido → arachno

closo-B6H6²⁻ · octahedron
drag to rotate
  • closo-B6H6²⁻: octahedron, six BH, no bridges.
  • Remove one vertex → nido-B5H9: square pyramid. The open square face carries 4 B–H–B bridges.
  • Remove an adjacent vertex → arachno-B4H10: butterfly. 4 bridges, and the two "wing-tip" B carry BH2 groups.
  • The extra H atoms (bridges, BH2) sit on the open face, where the removed vertices were.

Same skeletal electron count

B6H6²⁻, B5H9 and B4H10 all have 7 skeletal electron pairs, which is why they share one parent shape (Wade, Deck 6).

Das, Vol. 5, §10.12.3, Fig. 10.12.3.2; Williams (1971); models idealised from a regular octahedron (B–B 1.75 Å, B–Ht 1.19 Å, B–Hb 1.33 Å).
Use the buttons to step from closo to nido to arachno. Ask students where the bridging hydrogens appear: always around the opening. This is the most important structural pattern in borane chemistry.
Building with deltahedra

The icosahedron as parent: B12H12²⁻ → B10H14

closo-B12H12²⁻ · icosahedron
drag to rotate
  • B12H12²⁻: 12 BH units, Ih, no bridging H.
  • Remove two adjacent vertices and add 4 bridging H: B10H14, a basket with a six-membered open face.
  • Strictly, B10H14 is nido from the 11-vertex octadecahedron. The icosahedral view is a convenient picture.
  • B6H10 (pentagonal pyramid) is likewise the apical cap of an icosahedron.
Das, Vol. 5, §10.12.3, Fig. 10.12.3.5; Hawthorne (1967), p. 231; Mingos (2021), Fig. 16 (B10H14 as nido-11).
Both descriptions are in the literature. Das describes B10H14 by removing two vertices from the icosahedron; the Williams–Wade scheme classifies it as nido, derived from the 11-vertex closo shape. The atom set is the same; the point of difference is which parent is taken.

C
Part C: borane-by-borane. Each slide pairs an idealised 3D model with Hawthorne's drawing from the X-ray structure.
The individual boranes

Three kinds of hydrogen, one range of B–B distances

Featuretypical value
terminal B–H1.19 Å
symmetrical B–H–B bridge1.33 Å
unsymmetrical bridge, long sideup to 1.43 Å
B–B (most neighbours)1.70–1.86 Å
shortest B–B (B6H10, unbridged)1.60 Å
longest B···B (B10H14 5–10, 7–8)2.01 Å
  • Hydrogen occurs in three environments: terminal B–H, BH2 groups, and B–H–B bridges.
  • Bridges always lie on the open face of the cage. Closo anions have none.
  • B10H16, B18H22 and B20H16 contain borons with no terminal H at the points where cages join.
Hawthorne (1967), §5.2, p. 231.
These numbers recur through Decks 3–7. Note the spread of B–B distances: from 1.60 Å (an unbridged edge) to 2.01 Å (edges at the open face of B10H14).
The individual boranes

Tetraborane(10), arachno-B4H10: the butterfly

B4H10 (idealised)
drag to rotate
  • Two "hinge" BH and two "wing-tip" BH2, with 4 B–H–B bridges along the wing edges.
  • The bridges are unsymmetrical: the long B···H (1.43 Å) goes to the BH2 boron.
  • m.p. −120 °C, b.p. 16.1 °C. 11B NMR: triplet (2 BH2) and doublet (2 BH).
  • Made by storing B2H6 under pressure, or in a "hot–cold" reactor (120 °C / −78 °C) in 80–90 % yield.
Hawthorne (1967), §5.2 and §5.5F, pp. 231, 255; structure: C. E. Nordman, W. N. Lipscomb, J. Chem. Phys. 1953, 21, 1856; figure reproduced from Hawthorne Fig. 5.1(b).
B4H10 was Stock's first characterised borane (1912). Its butterfly shape is the arachno form derived from the octahedron (previous Part). Warming to 60 °C converts it mainly to B5H11.
The individual boranes

Pentaborane(9), nido-B5H9: the square pyramid

B5H9 · C4v (idealised)
drag to rotate
  • Apical BH over a square of four basal BH, with 4 bridges on the basal edges.
  • b.p. 58.4 °C, m.p. −46.1 °C. Very thermally stable, thanks to its delocalised bonding.
  • 11B NMR: doublet of area 1 (apex, high field) and doublet of area 4 (base). 1H: bridges at highest field.
  • Made by pyrolysis of B2H6 with H2 at ≈ 250 °C. It ignites spontaneously in air.
Hawthorne (1967), §5.5G, pp. 258–259; structure: W. J. Dulmage, W. N. Lipscomb, Acta Crystallogr. 1952, 5, 260; figure from Hawthorne Fig. 5.1(c).
B5H9 is the nido form from the octahedron. The 1:4 pattern in the 11B NMR spectrum is a quick fingerprint. It was the borane most studied as a high-energy fuel (see the Did-you-know).
The individual boranes

Pentaborane(11), arachno-B5H11: an open pyramid

B5H11 (idealised)
drag to rotate
  • Apical BH2 over an open base of four B (two BH2 ends, two BH), with 3 bridges.
  • One apical H points into the cage. It shows no spin coupling to its own boron, which suggests it partly bridges to the base.
  • b.p. 63 °C, m.p. −123.3 °C. Short-lived at room temperature.
  • It is the first isolable product of B2H6 pyrolysis at about 100 °C.
Hawthorne (1967), §5.2 and §5.5H, pp. 231, 262–263; structure: L. R. Lavine, W. N. Lipscomb, J. Chem. Phys. 1954, 22, 614; figure from Hawthorne Fig. 5.1(d).
B5H11 shows how subtle the boundary between terminal and bridging hydrogen can be: the interior apical H behaves partly as a bridge. It is an important intermediate in diborane pyrolysis.
The individual boranes

Hexaborane(10), nido-B6H10: the pentagonal pyramid

B6H10 (idealised)
drag to rotate
  • Apical BH over a pentagon of five BH, with 4 bridges. One basal edge is unbridged.
  • That unbridged B–B is 1.60 Å, the shortest B–B in any borane.
  • 11B NMR shows all five basal B as equivalent: the bridging H migrate rapidly around the base.
  • b.p. 108 °C, m.p. −63.2 °C. Made from B5H11 with a weak base (e.g. diglyme): 2 B5H11 → B6H10 + 2 B2H6.
Hawthorne (1967), §5.2 and §5.5I, pp. 231, 263–264; structure: F. L. Hirshfeld, K. Eriks, R. E. Dickerson, E. L. Lippert, W. N. Lipscomb, J. Chem. Phys. 1958, 28, 56; figure from Hawthorne Fig. 5.1(e).
Fluxionality: the 11B spectrum is averaged because the four bridges hop around the five basal edges. This is our first example of a fluxional borane; more in Deck 5.
The individual boranes

Decaborane(14), nido-B10H14: the basket

B10H14 · C2v (idealised)
drag to rotate
  • Ten BH units in a boat-shaped basket, with 4 bridges on the open hexagonal face (B5–B6, B6–B7, B8–B9, B9–B10).
  • B5–B10 and B7–B8 are long (2.01 Å), and the bridges are unsymmetrical.
  • White crystalline solid, m.p. 99.7 °C, b.p. 213 °C. Stable in air, the only neutral borane that is.
  • Made by pyrolysis of B2H6 near 100–200 °C. It was the first borane solved by X-ray (1950).
Hawthorne (1967), §5.2 and §5.5O, pp. 231, 265; J. S. Kasper, C. M. Lucht, D. Harker, Acta Crystallogr. 1950, 3, 436; air stability: Das, §10.12.8; figure from Hawthorne Fig. 5.1(h).
B10H14 is the most versatile borane: the starting point for B10H10 2−, the carboranes (Deck 7) and much of Deck 5. Its bridging hydrogens are relatively acidic.
Did you know?

A "stable" borane that becomes a high explosive

  • Decaborane(14) is air-stable and can be sublimed and recrystallised like an organic solid.
  • But it forms explosive mixtures with halogenated hydrocarbons. Saturated B10H14 in CCl4 is shock-sensitive and energetically equivalent to a high explosive.
  • Halogenated solvents are therefore "scrupulously avoided" in decaborane work. It is a lesson in reading the safety literature before choosing a solvent.
⚠

B10H14 + CCl4

Reducing hydride cage + oxidising C–Cl bonds in close contact.

Hawthorne (1967), §5.5O.1, p. 265.
A safety aside. Boranes are strong reducing agents; mixed with oxidising halocarbons they become explosive.
The individual boranes

Larger and fused (conjuncto) boranes

Boraneclassnotes
B8H12nido*from B2H6 + B5H9 + H2 in a discharge. *Closer to arachno-B9H15, the known exception
B9H15arachnom.p. 2.6 °C; structure solved before its chemistry
B10H16conjunctotwo B5H8 joined apex–apex (B–B 1.74 Å): 2 B5H9 → B10H16 + H2 (discharge)
n- and iso-B18H22conjunctofirst isomeric boranes: two B10 units sharing an edge, with 7-coordinate B at the junction

Hawthorne (1967), §5.2 and §5.5L–S, pp. 231, 264–286; B8H12 exception: Mingos (2021), p. 26; figures from Hawthorne Fig. 5.1.
Conjuncto boranes are made by joining smaller cages: by a two-centre B–B bond (B10H16), by sharing an edge (B18H22), or by fusion (B20H16). The B18H22 isomers were historically important as the first isomeric pair.
The individual boranes

The closo anions: unusually stable

B10H10²⁻ · D4d
drag to rotate
B12H12²⁻ · Ih
drag to rotate
  • B10H10²⁻: bicapped square antiprism (8 equatorial + 2 apical BH). Its structure was first deduced from 11B NMR, then confirmed by X-ray.
  • B12H12²⁻: regular icosahedron with a fully delocalised 2− charge.
  • "Aromatic" boranes: kinetically stable to hydrolysis and even to strong acid. They are the closo end-point of Williams' series.
  • Chemistry and carboranes: Deck 7.
Hawthorne (1967), §5.3 and §5.6, pp. 232–233, 286; Das, §10.12.8(c); models idealised.
Brief preview only. Contrast their stability with the reactive neutral boranes; Deck 6 explains this electronically, and Deck 7 covers the chemistry.

Making boranes

Diborane: from Stock's boride to modern reagents

RouteEquationNote
Stock (1912–13)Mg3B2 + HCl(aq) → B4H10 …; B4H10 → B2H6 + …low yield; historic
Schlesinger & Burg (1931)2 BCl3 + 5 H2 → B2H5Cl + 5 HCl; 6 B2H5Cl ⇌ 5 B2H6 + 2 BCl3electric discharge
Hydride + BX38 BF3 + 6 NaH → 6 NaBF4 + B2H6Das

In practice

Diborane is often generated as needed, or replaced by its adducts H3B·THF and H3B·SMe2 (Deck 2), which are safer to store and handle.

Das, §10.12.7(a)–(b); H. I. Schlesinger, A. B. Burg, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1931, 53, 4321; Schlesinger–Brown route as in course PPT (slide 91); Stone (1955).
Check the stoichiometry of each equation with the class. The NaH/BF3 equation is a good balancing exercise (Na, B, F and H all balance).
Making boranes

Heat diborane: one starting material, many boranes

Products are separated by fractional condensation on the vacuum line (Deck 1). Above ≈ 700 °C every borane decomposes to boron and H2.

Hawthorne (1967), §5.5F–O, pp. 255–265; Stone (1955), p. 175; Das, §10.12.7(c).
Read the chart from left to right: mild conditions give the arachno boranes B4H10 and B5H11; hotter conditions, especially with H2, give the more stable nido boranes B5H9 and B10H14. This is the nido-over-arachno stability pattern in synthetic form.
Making boranes

How pyrolysis builds cages: BH3 gain, H2 loss

  • Step 1: B2H6 ⇌ 2 BH3. Reactive BH3 is the building block.
  • Step 2: BH3 + B2H6 → B3H9 → B3H7 + H2. Unstable B3H7 (Schaeffer) is the key intermediate.
  • Step 3: B3H7 + B2H6 → B5H11 + H2; B3H7 + BH3 → B4H10.
  • Equilibria link the products: B2H6 + 2 B4H10 ⇌ 2 B5H11 + 2 H2 (Schlesinger).
  • In (BH)n(BH3)x terms: each step adds BH3 or converts BH3 → BH + H2.
Das, §10.12.7(c); Hawthorne (1967), §5.5F–H (Schaeffer's B3H7/B4H8 intermediates; Schlesinger equilibrium).
This is a simplified mechanism, but it captures the logic: boranes grow by adding BH3 units and lose hydrogen to close up. Students can check each equation balances in B and H.

Balance check

5 B4H10 = B20H50; 2 B5H9 + 5 B2H6 + H2 = B20H18+30+2 = B20H50 ✓

Hawthorne (1967), §5.5F, G, I, P, S, pp. 255–286.
Each conversion illustrates a type of process: closing up (arachno → nido), growing, joining and degrading. Have students balance one equation themselves.
Making boranes

Controlled cage growth: remove H⁺, insert BH3

  • Bridging H are acidic. A strong base (KH) removes one as H⁺, leaving a B–B bond in the anion.
  • That B–B bond is electron-rich and acts as the site for electrophilic insertion of BH3 (from ½ B2H6).
  • Protonation (HCl) then releases H2 and the larger neutral borane.

B4H10 + KH → K[B4H9] + H2
K[B4H9] + ½ B2H6 → K[B5H12]
K[B5H12] + HCl → B5H11 + H2 + KCl

B5H9 + KH → K[B5H8] + H2 → (+ ½ B2H6) K[B6H11] → (+ HCl) B6H10

Das, §10.12.7(d) (equations); method developed by S. G. Shore and co-workers in the 1970s (see Greenwood & Earnshaw, 2nd edn, §6.7.3).
This is a rational, stepwise way to add one boron at a time, much better controlled than pyrolysis. It also shows two chemical properties that recur in Deck 5: the Brønsted acidity of bridging H, and the nucleophilic B–B bond of the conjugate base.
Making boranes

Making the closo anions, and NaBH4

Base-promoted cage closure (≈ 150 °C)

B10H14 + 2 R3N → [R3NH]2[B10H10] + H2

6 B2H6 + 2 R3N → [R3NH]2[B12H12] + 11 H2

nido or arachno + base + heat → the most stable closo cage, with loss of H2.

NaBH4

laboratory2 NaH + B2H6 → 2 NaBH4 (diglyme)
laboratory4 NaH + BCl3 → NaBH4 + 3 NaCl
Schlesinger–BrownB(OMe)3 + 4 NaH → NaBH4 + 3 NaOMe (250–270 °C)
Bayer processNa2B4O7 + 7 SiO2 + 16 Na + 8 H2 → 4 NaBH4 + 7 Na2SiO3
Das, §10.12.7(e) and NaBH4 preparation; Hawthorne (1967), §5.6; Schlesinger–Brown: J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1953, 75, 186.
Balance check for B12H12 2−: 6 B2H6 contains 36 H; 12 stay on boron, 2 go to R3NH+, and 22 leave as 11 H2. The Bayer process starts from borax, the oldest boron material in this course.
Did you know?

The boranes nearly became jet fuel

  • Boranes release about 1.5 times the heat of comparable hydrocarbons on combustion.
  • In the 1950s the USA ran a large "high-energy fuels" programme ("zip fuels") on boranes and alkylboranes for aircraft and rockets. Hawthorne calls it "an all out effort".
  • It failed in practice: solid B2O3 fouled engines, and boranes are toxic and pyrophoric. The chemistry it produced, including the polyhedral anions and the carboranes, became its real legacy.

B2H6 + 3 O2
→ B2O3(s) + 3 H2O

a very exothermic reaction, but with a solid product

Hawthorne (1967), §5.1, p. 223; Das, §10.12.8(a).
An example of applied research that failed in its goal but transformed a field: the polyhedral boranes and carboranes of Decks 6–7 came out of this programme.
Summary

Key points

  • Formula → class: BnHn²⁻ closo, BnHn+4 nido, BnHn+6 arachno, BnHn+8 hypho; fused cages are conjuncto.
  • Shapes come from the closo deltahedra, n = 5–12, by removing the most connected vertex (nido) and then an adjacent one (arachno). This is Williams (1971).
  • Bridging H and BH2 groups sit on the open face. B–Ht 1.19, B–Hb 1.33, B–B 1.60–2.01 Å.
  • Key structures: B4H10 butterfly, B5H9 square pyramid, B5H11 open pyramid, B6H10 pentagonal pyramid, B10H14 basket.
  • Synthesis: B2H6 pyrolysis (BH3 gain, H2 loss), deprotonation–BH3 insertion, discharge, and base-promoted closure to the closo anions.
Hawthorne (1967); Das, §10.12; Williams (1971); Mingos (2021).
Ask students to classify B8H12, B9H15 and B10H16 from their formulas, then compare with the structures.
Check your understanding

Questions (press → to reveal each answer)

1. Classify B6H10, B9H15 and B5H12⁻.
B6H10 = BnHn+4: nido. B9H15 = BnHn+6: arachno. B5H12⁻ ≡ B5H13 = BnHn+8: hypho.
2. Which closo shape is the parent of B5H9 and B4H10?
The octahedron (B6H6²⁻), with one and two adjacent vertices removed respectively.
3. Why does B6H10 show only one 11B signal for its five basal B?
The four bridging H migrate rapidly around the five basal edges, averaging the basal environments on the NMR timescale.
4. Balance: 6 B2H6 + 2 R3N → [R3NH]2[B12H12] + ? H2
36 H on the left; 12 + 2 retained; 22 H = 11 H2.
Based on this deck.
Allow a minute per question.
